title: WCAG and Accessibility Testing
summary: WCAG's POUR principles and A/AA/AAA levels are the standard nearly every legal and procurement requirement points to, but automated tools only catch a fraction of it. Learn the split between what tools catch and what needs a real manual pass.

slides.markdown:
WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) is the technical standard underlying nearly every legal accessibility requirement discussed in [Why Accessibility Matters](why-accessibility-matters) — the ADA, the European Accessibility Act, and most vendor security/procurement questionnaires all point to WCAG conformance as their practical bar, rather than defining their own criteria from scratch.

This topic covers what WCAG actually says (the POUR principles and the A/AA/AAA conformance levels), and — arguably more useful day to day — the honest split between what automated tools like axe can catch and what genuinely requires a human pass. Teams that treat a clean automated scan as "fully accessible" are making a specific, well-documented mistake this topic exists to prevent.

slides.subTitle: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust
slides.markdown:
Every WCAG success criterion falls under one of four principles, and knowing which one a given rule serves makes the whole spec easier to reason about instead of memorizing rules as an unordered list:

- **Perceivable** — information must be presentable in ways users can perceive, regardless of sense. Alt text for images (perceivable without sight), captions for audio (perceivable without hearing), sufficient color contrast.
- **Operable** — interface components must be operable by any input method. Keyboard accessibility, no content that flashes enough to trigger seizures, enough time to complete timed actions.
- **Understandable** — information and UI operation must be understandable. Consistent navigation across pages, clear error identification, predictable behavior (a control shouldn't unexpectedly change context just from receiving focus).
- **Robust** — content must be robust enough to work with a wide variety of user agents, including current and future assistive technology. Valid, well-formed markup that parses correctly; this is largely why semantic HTML and correct ARIA matter — malformed or misused markup is the most common way to fail Robust.

When an audit finding doesn't immediately suggest a fix, naming which POUR principle it violates often clarifies the actual requirement being tested.

slides.subTitle: A, AA, AAA
slides.markdown:
WCAG defines three conformance levels, each a strict superset of requirements over the one below it — meeting AA requires also meeting every A criterion:

- **Level A** — the baseline; failing it means the content is inaccessible to some users in a fundamental way (missing alt text, keyboard traps with no escape).
- **Level AA** — the level almost every real-world legal requirement and company policy actually targets; adds things like a 4.5:1 text contrast ratio, resizable text up to 200% without loss of content, and consistent navigation.
- **Level AAA** — the strictest level, and explicitly, in the spec's own words, not recommended as a general policy for entire sites, because some AAA criteria (like a 7:1 contrast ratio, or sign-language interpretation for all video) aren't achievable for all types of content without compromising the content itself.

When someone asks "what level should we target," the answer for the overwhelming majority of products is **AA** — it's the level legal frameworks reference, the level most audits check against, and the level that's actually achievable without the content-specific compromises AAA sometimes demands.

slides.sectionTitle: What automated tools can and can't catch
slides.markdown:
Automated tools (axe, Lighthouse's accessibility audit, WAVE) are excellent at checking things with an objective, computable answer: missing `alt` attributes, insufficient color contrast ratios, missing form labels, invalid ARIA attribute values, duplicate ids. These are genuinely valuable — cheap, fast, and easy to wire into CI — and catch real, common bugs.

What they structurally cannot check: whether alt text is actually *meaningful* (an image with `alt="image"` passes every automated check while being useless), whether a custom widget's keyboard interaction makes sense, whether a live region announces at a reasonable time relative to the change it describes, whether reading order matches visual order, or the exact staleness bug from [ARIA Roles, States, and Properties](aria-roles-states-properties) — a stale `aria-expanded` is syntactically valid and invisible to any tool inspecting a static snapshot.

Industry estimates commonly cited put automated coverage around **20–40% of WCAG success criteria** — a genuinely useful floor, and nowhere close to a ceiling.

slides.sectionTitle: The split between automated and manual coverage
slides.markdown:
Picture the full set of WCAG success criteria as one circle. Automated tools reliably cover a meaningful but minority slice — objectively computable things like contrast ratios, missing alt attributes, invalid markup, missing labels. A much larger slice requires actual human judgment: whether alt text is meaningful rather than just present, whether a custom widget's keyboard behavior is sensible, whether reading order matches visual order, whether a live region's timing is right, whether error messages are genuinely clear rather than just technically present.

A small remaining slice needs specialized tools or hardware entirely outside a typical dev workflow — screen-flash/seizure-risk analysis for video content is the standard example, requiring purpose-built analysis tools most teams don't have on hand for routine development.

slides.subTitle: Keyboard-only and screen-reader testing
slides.markdown:
A minimal, genuinely useful manual pass doesn't require becoming a screen reader power user overnight — it requires running through the same core flows twice, once per method, on top of whatever automated scan already ran:

- **Keyboard-only**: unplug the mouse (or just don't touch it) and Tab through every interactive flow — can you reach everything, in a sensible order, with a visible focus indicator at every stop, and does every custom widget respond to the keys it should ([Keyboard Navigation and Focus](keyboard-navigation-and-focus) covers this in depth)?
- **Screen reader**: turn on VoiceOver (Mac/iOS, built in — Cmd+F5) or NVDA (Windows, free) and navigate the same flows by ear, eyes closed if you can manage it. Does every image's alt text make sense out of context? Does every form error get announced? Does the page's heading/landmark structure let you jump around sensibly rather than forcing linear reading?

This pass takes on the order of 30–60 minutes for a typical feature, not days, and reliably surfaces issues (meaningless alt text, a keyboard trap, a silent form error) that a clean automated scan gives zero indication of.

slides.sectionTitle: Wiring an automated check into CI

slides.markdown:
A team ships a feature with a completely clean axe report and reasonably concludes the accessibility work is finished — the tool found nothing, so there's nothing left to fix. In practice this reliably ships real, sometimes severe issues: a custom dropdown with perfect ARIA roles and zero keyboard support (every attribute is valid, so nothing gets flagged, even though it's completely unusable without a mouse), an `alt="photo"` on every image on the page (present, so it passes the missing-alt check, while conveying nothing useful to anyone who can't see the photo), or a live region that fires so late after its triggering event that a screen reader user has already moved on and misses it entirely.

None of these are automated-tool bugs — they're the tool correctly doing exactly what it's designed to do, which is check markup validity and a fixed set of computable rules, not judge whether the experience actually works for a real user of assistive technology.

The corrective habit: treat a clean automated scan as clearing the floor, then run the manual keyboard and screen-reader pass from earlier in this topic before calling anything "accessible," not as an optional extra step reserved for a dedicated audit cycle.

WCAG criteria are numbered `<principle>.<guideline>.<criterion>` — for instance, **1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)** sits under Principle 1 (Perceivable), Guideline 4 (Distinguishable), and is the third criterion under that guideline, requiring a 4.5:1 contrast ratio for normal text at Level AA (3:1 for large text, defined as 18pt+ or 14pt+ bold).

Each criterion also states its level (A/AA/AAA) directly, which is often the fastest way to answer "do we need to fix this" in a real prioritization conversation — a Level A finding is close to non-negotiable, an AA finding matches the target level almost every team should be meeting, and an AAA finding is worth evaluating case by case rather than treated as required.

Being able to look up a specific criterion (the W3C's Understanding WCAG documents explain each one with examples) rather than working from memory or vague recollection is a normal, expected part of doing this work well — nobody has all several hundred criteria memorized.

"How would you audit this page for accessibility" is testing whether you have an actual process, not whether you can recite WCAG criteria from memory. A strong answer walks through layers in order: run an automated scan first (fast, catches the objective floor — contrast, missing labels, invalid markup), then a keyboard-only pass through every interactive flow, then a screen-reader pass through the same flows focusing on whether announcements make sense and arrive at a reasonable time, then a targeted check of anything the page does that's unusual (a custom widget, dynamic content, video) against the specific WCAG criteria most relevant to it.

The weakest answer here is "I'd run axe and fix whatever it finds" — technically a valid first step, but incomplete on its own, and naming that limitation explicitly ("and then I'd do a manual pass, because axe only catches a fraction of what matters") is exactly the signal that separates someone who understands the tooling's real limits from someone repeating a tool name as if it were a complete methodology.

slides.sectionTitle: Where this fits in a real team's workflow
slides.markdown:
In a healthy team, none of this lives as a separate "accessibility phase" bolted onto the end of a project — automated checks run in CI on every PR as a baseline gate, semantic HTML and correct ARIA are just how components get built day to day (the earlier topics in this group), and a manual keyboard/screen-reader pass happens for genuinely new or complex UI patterns before they ship widely, the same way a new component might get a design review or a performance check.

A periodic, deeper external audit still has real value — a specialist with more assistive-technology experience than the team, tools for the harder-to-check cases (seizure-risk analysis, deep screen-reader-combination testing), and enough distance from the code to catch what familiarity blinds an internal team to — but it should be finding the remaining edge cases, not doing the basic work the team's own process should already have caught.
